strengths: Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse RL domains (discrete, continuous, offline, language-based, streaming) with rigorous statistical methodology (IQM, 95% confidence intervals), demonstrating consistent performance improvements
Elegant and simple solution that is easy to implement and understand, with 40-50% parameter reduction while achieving or exceeding target-based performance
Strong and consistent empirical results: iS-DQN K=9 achieves 106% of target-based DQN on Atari CNN+LN, closes performance gaps across multiple domains, and often outperforms baselines
Insightful mechanistic analysis (Section 5.6) providing intuition via gradient similarity, target churn metric, and effective rank analysis
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, experimental setup, individual learning curves, and implementation details in appendices
Addresses genuine practical problem of memory constraints limiting scalability to edge devices and large networks, with clear motivation
Demonstrates orthogonality to existing techniques (LayerNorm, BatchNorm, MellowMax), showing broad applicability
Comprehensive ablation studies examining target update period, number of Bellman updates, architecture variations, and mixed-precision training
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is straightforward parameter sharing with frozen linear head; heavily relies on existing iterated Q-learning framework (Vincent et al. 2025b), making this primarily an engineering contribution rather than algorithmic innovation

Hyperparameter K introduces significant tuning burden: optimal values vary dramatically across domains (K=9 for CNN, K=49 for IMPALA, K=3 for streaming), contradicting resource-efficiency motivation; D.4 meta-learning reveals equal weights converge to optimal, questioning whether learning K heads adds value

Incomplete theoretical understanding: lacks principled explanation for why K varies across architectures; no convergence guarantees or theoretical justification; architecture-dependence of K deserves deeper analysis beyond 'representation richness'

Weak results in several domains limit generality: SAC continuous control shows K=9 only matches K=1 and requires ad-hoc 0.25 discounting factor; streaming RL shows only 10% improvements on 7 games with K>3 hurting performance; single Wordle task with modest improvements

Ad-hoc design choices without principled justification: 0.25 discounting factor in Section 5.3 lacks theoretical motivation; loss aggregation strategy borrowed from Vincent et al. without exploring alternatives; meta-learning aggregation weights (D.4) implemented but not adopted

Computational cost not reduced: training time and FLOPs identical to target-based approaches (Figure 11); benefits limited to memory and performance, not speed; severely limits applicability in latency-critical scenarios
Inference memory not reduced: paper acknowledges same memory footprint during deployment as target-based approaches, a significant practical limitation for edge deployment applications

Limited baseline comparisons: MellowMax comparison restricted to 2 games in appendix; comprehensive comparison with other target-free stabilization methods lacking; recent methods like Hendawy et al. (2026) mentioned but not compared
